title: The consequences of the US midterm elections
author: IISS

Online Analysis6th November 2026

The consequences of the US midterm electionsOn 3 November 2026, American voters delivered a resounding defeat to President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in midterm congressional and gubernatorial elections. Senior Fellows in the IISS US Foreign Policy and Transatlantic Affairs research programme provide their views on the significance of these elections.

US President Donald Trump walks off stage at a midterm campaign rally in Corinth, Mississippi on 26 October 2026. Photo by Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images

Congress changes hands and Trump’s presidency narrows
Paul Fraioli
In winning control of both chambers of Congress, Democrats delivered a sharp rebuke to Republicans amid discontentment on the issues of government corruption, the high cost of living and the war against Iran. In exit polls, voters called these three issues ‘crucial’ at rates of 55%, 49% and 34%, respectively. In early 2026, Democrats appeared to have a one-in-three chance of gaining control of the Senate. Yet the party may start the next congress controlling as many as 56 seats out of 100, winning traditional Grand Old Party (GOP) strongholds in Texas and Kansas.
From 3 January 2027 to January 2029, Democrats will have the power to use federal funding deadlines to extract concessions from the White House and investigate the administration and companies that have dealt closely with it since 2025. Control of the Senate also gives Democrats the power to reject President Donald Trump’s nominees to judicial and senior-executive posts. Companies that cultivated personal relationships with the White House now must consider both how to manage relations with congressional Democrats and how to operate in a markedly different political environment. Those with federal contracts or deals negotiated under Trump should expect closer scrutiny of how these arrangements were made.
The artificial intelligence (AI) data-centre build-out faces new headwinds, particularly at the state and local levels. Texas – an important and hitherto development-friendly jurisdiction for this sector – elected a Democratic Party governor who campaigned on a data-centre moratorium. Voters chose to limit or restrict data-centre development in nearly all of the approximately 41 related ballot measures nationwide. Democrats regard their sceptical stance on AI and data centres as having contributed to their electoral success – a signpost for their positioning in the 2028 elections – which has lowered future expectations among investors regarding AI capital investment in a sector already facing correction risk.
Trump said prior to the elections that he would accept the results. On Election Day evening, he posted 11 times on Truth Social, which included five attacks on Fox News and fellow Republicans, and four touts about his own electoral prowess, claiming that Republicans would have won had he been on the ballot. Before the new congress convenes, Trump can press the outgoing Senate to confirm judges and may choose to support or file lawsuits in close races and launch further prosecutions over alleged voter fraud.
Trump – perhaps the US president least suited, constitutionally, to serving as a lame duck in recent memory – will give some indication in the coming weeks as to the kind of lame duck he will be. He may pivot from acquiescence to using the tools of the Executive Branch to launch a maximalist fight against Democrats taking power in January. This would be difficult to sustain, however, given the degree to which Trump’s influence among Republicans will wane in response to the election drubbing. It is virtually certain that he will fight, wherever possible, the Democrats’ legislative exercises of authority once the next congress is seated.
The Republican succession contest will intensify in the next six months as prospective candidates jockey for position and the future of Trumpism begins to take shape. The morning after Election Day, Vice President JD Vance wrote on X that ‘the reason we lost is the war’, giving this issue the most weight rather than corruption or high prices, as voters noted. Trump, without room to advance his domestic agenda in Congress, will probably turn further towards foreign policy – seeking, for example, to impose his vision on international economic and alliance issues to an even greater extent – and to projects that bear his personal imprint, like the many construction projects ongoing and planned in Washington DC.show more

Key coordinates of foreign policy unlikely to change
Benjamin Rhode
Since his emergence as a presidential candidate a decade ago, it has been clear to many observers that President Donald Trump’s understanding of international affairs largely reflects his views of domestic politics (and life more generally).
For example, some initially seemed surprised when Trump and his followers denigrated Washington’s European allies. But to Trump, many of the governments of these European so-called allies closely resemble the Democrats in their political worldview, and thus are portrayed as essentially parasitic, liberal globalists who supposedly espouse open borders, disarmament and the appeasement of Islamists. They therefore serve as a useful foil in American domestic politics, providing an example of what the United States would presumably look like were the Democrats to get their way. Since December 2025, encouraging the replacement of these liberal governments with far-right alternatives has been the Trump administration’s stated policy. Similarly, within MAGA circles, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine is frequently depicted not as a heroic defender of an invaded country but as a corrupt hero of the Democrats, who in reality started (or at least provoked) the conflict with Russia, failed to hand over the imagined evidence of former president Joe Biden’s family corruption in Ukraine when requested by President Trump in 2019 and in fact was the cause of Trump’s first impeachment. Relatedly, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin and China’s President Xi Jinping are not depicted as ideological enemies of a democratic US, but as strong leaders with whom deals can be made.   Trump has held these opinions for many years, and even if he acknowledges that the war against Iran contributed directly and indirectly to Republican electoral losses, at 80 years old he himself is unlikely to change his basic worldview. While Democratic control of Congress may indeed have some concrete and possibly significant effects on the mechanics of US defence and foreign policy, as my colleagues describe, at least in the short term the broader guiding coordinates of Trumpian foreign policy will remain essentially the same.
The scenario in which around a dozen Republican senators combine with Democratic colleagues to essentially threaten Trump to either moderate or face conviction by the requisite two-thirds majority remains highly unlikely. Senate Republicans were unwilling to convict Trump when he was impeached in January 2021 following the 6 January riots; they are less likely to do so now.
A plausible scenario is one in which this electoral defeat does not moderate Trump’s foreign policy, but in fact makes it more impulsive. During the run-up to these midterm elections, in which President Trump exhorted voters to ‘pretend [he] is on the ballot’, he responded to widespread concerns about artificial intelligence (AI) by declaring that anyone who did not refer to it as ‘superior intelligence’ was ‘the enemy’. In response to anger about energy prices, Trump preferred to broker an ineffectual diesel deal with Russia, while attempting to scapegoat Zelenskyy for continuing the war, rather than end the primary cause of higher prices: the conflict with Iran. This suggests that he is not likely to moderate his behaviour now that he has no further elections ahead of him, especially since, as my colleague Paul Fraioli suggests above, foreign policy will be one sphere in which he faces fewer political constraints.
In the longer term, it is of course likely that the scale of this defeat will prompt those Republicans seeking to succeed Trump to try to distance themselves from unpopular aspects of his foreign policy while still retaining the support of the MAGA faithful. But President Trump will remain the commander-in-chief until January 2029. Whether the US would honour its commitments to NATO, for example, remains his decision. As the journalist Edward Lucas asked recently, who really believes that Trump would be more likely to offer a firm response to a Russian incursion into NATO territory because the Democrats control Congress?show more

Earthquake
Dana H. Allin
The political earthquake that struck the United States on Tuesday was both a clear and astonishing electoral rebuke of President Donald Trump and a corrective to the commonplace idea that foreign policy plays a negligible role in American electoral politics. Foreign policy across multiple dimensions played a huge role: the Iran war, Trump’s rampant tariffs against allies, his immigration and mass-deportation policies, and the unrestrained imperial presidency writ large at home and abroad. That the pain point for Americans’ reaction to the war against Iran was the consequent soaring gasoline and diesel prices only underscores that foreign and domestic policies are almost always intertwined. Moreover, opinion polls showed the Iran war to be hugely unpopular even before the economic effects hit home.
This was the biggest landslide victory for an opposition party in America since 1974, the post-Watergate midterm election. In that case, the Democrats already held both houses of Congress. But the comparison of 2026 with 1974 is germane, for two reasons. Firstly, there is the often-noted comparison between the worldviews of Trump and former president Richard Nixon, extending to rampant norm-breaking and presidential lawlessness. We should treat this analogy with some care. Although the moral costs of Nixon’s policies in Cambodia, Chile, East Pakistan (now Bangladesh), Vietnam and elsewhere were high, there is a strong argument that Nixon left the US in a stronger strategic position than he found it upon taking office in 1969. Nixon, in any event, had a concept of the West that he intended to defend and the strategic acumen to do so. It would be a stretch to say the same about Trump. Secondly, 1974 suggests caution about projecting forward a Democratic ascendancy. It is true that the post-Watergate class of newly elected Democrats had a substantial influence on the political culture and policies of subsequent decades. It is also true that two years later, Democrat Jimmy Carter, espousing a counter-Nixonian commitment to neo-Wilsonian human rights and international law, won the presidency. However, ‘the Carter administration turned out to be a parenthesis inside 20 years of Republican presidents’, as I wrote more than 30 years ago. Moreover, Carter’s neo-Wilsonianism, as an intellectual and moral template, was swept away by the force of events such as the Iranian seizure of the US embassy and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, as well as the neoconservative reaction that helped carry Ronald Reagan into the White House in 1981.
Surveying the Republican wreckage after a bit more than 24 hours – as I write, the contested senate seat in Mississippi may be on the verge of capture by an African-American Democrat – it is hard to see any Republican equivalent of the neoconservative defence intellectuals who powered Reaganism. Vice President JD Vance made a gesture in the opposite direction on 4 November, posting a list of reasons for the Republican defeat that started with the Iran war and ended with America’s relationship with Israel. However, Vance will be in a difficult position for the next two years if he tries to run for president on a right-wing version of presidential candidate George McGovern’s 1972 ‘Come Home, America’ refrain, while concurrently avoiding a damaging break with the president who chose him.
Victorious Democrats, meanwhile, will have to cope with a vast gap between great expectations and limited power while Trump remains president. Furthermore, the force of events for the rest of this decade – think of the pace of artificial-intelligence (AI) development – may well rival or exceed the turmoil that brought down Jimmy Carter.show more

Lame-duck militarism or aggressive oversight? Post-election defence policy
Jonathan D. Caverley
Both Vice President JD Vance and President Donald Trump blamed the decisive Democratic victory in the midterm elections on the administration’s war against Iran. What are the implications of the lame-duck Congress, and the incoming divided federal government, for the conduct of the war and for defence policy generally?
The war is certainly unpopular. In one nationally representative poll, 63% of respondents agreed that the United States made the ‘wrong decision on Iran’ and 74% stated that the conflict was a ‘crucial’ or ‘major’ factor in their vote. Still, one should not overstate the effect. Foreign policy rarely drives American electoral outcomes. The war’s biggest effect was likely indirect through rising prices. 40% of respondents in an AP poll said the economy was the most important issue, another 30% chose the state of democracy, and very few respondents had foreign policy as their top issue. The Democrats will likely focus accordingly, and approach security policy through these lenses. Lame-duck presidents, especially when their domestic agenda is stymied, tend to become more active in foreign policy in the last years of their administrations. Iran and Ukraine
While Trump raised the prospects of escalation against Iran after the midterms, the scale of the Democratic victory, not to mention the ongoing Israeli negotiations over a new government coalition, probably makes this less likely. It is unclear what remaining incentive the administration has to prolong the conflict, and the surviving Republican caucus would no doubt prefer lower energy prices.
A Democratic-controlled legislature is unlikely to bring much relief to Ukraine, given that Trump has waived most of the sanctions on Russia required by the 2026 Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, passed by a Republican-controlled Congress. No matter who is in charge, defence acquisitions will focus on rebuilding the United States’ severely depleted munitions stocks, and that alone is currently more than the US defence-industrial base can handle. Any new influx of American support for Ukraine will be modest.
Defence budgeting and authorisation
Buying weapons requires an appropriations act. The new Congress can hardly make less progress on developing and funding defence policy than the current one. The federal government’s continuing resolution expires on 11 December, and another continuing resolution until at least the new Congress is sworn in is the most likely next phase (the worst case is a complete government shutdown). The Trump administration requested US$1.5 trillion in defence spending in April, which does not factor in the cost of the war against Iran. But the full House has still not voted on the defence appropriations bill, and the Senate version has not even made it out of committee. The top line was probably always going to be unrealistic, but the armed services and industry seem to accept that a Democratic legislature is even less likely to fund it.
More unusually, and perhaps more consequentially, the future of the 2027 National Defense Authorization bill, the annual policy legislation necessary for much of the Department of War’s activities, also remains uncertain. The House passed its version in July, but the Senate has yet to pass its own version. Normally a relatively bipartisan process – Congress has passed a National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) each of the past 65 years – the parties are deadlocked over whether the Iran war can continue without a formal authorisation from Congress. While adding this to the bill will likely pass in both houses next year if not this, Trump could plausibly veto it. Without a withdrawal from the conflict, the divided government will make a successful NDAA even less likely.
Oversight
Both the House and Senate can be expected to use their subpoena power, hearings and even impeachment proceedings; the incoming Chair of the House Oversight Committee, Robert Garcia, responded to the Democratic wave with a two-word post: ‘lawyer up’. On top of this, a Democratic-controlled Senate can make sure that no presidential appointments are confirmed. So while Secretary of War Pete Hegseth could resign or be removed from office, the path to confirming his replacement is therefore unclear.
Given that Elon Musk spent over half a billion dollars in support of Republican midterm candidates, his time at the head of the Department of Government Efficiency, and the recent throttling of Starlink access to Ukrainian forces, there is good partisan and national security logic to opening an investigation. Moreover, there is a general perception that many of the contracts awarded to relatively new entrants into defence acquisition, from rare earths to uncrewed systems, have been awarded in a less-than-transparent fashion. The possibility of increased oversight, combined with the realisation that procurement dollars are unlikely to provide the return that venture capital investors require, is likely to put pressure on the large numbers of American defence tech start-ups.show more

Can the Democrats restrain President Trump?
Jonathan Stevenson
For President Donald Trump’s many and growing opponents, the Republican Party’s epic shellacking in the midterms brings vindication and trepidation. American voters have confirmed that they reject all major aspects of Trumpism – coercive and ineffective economic policy, capricious foreign policy, the brutal conduct of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), unprecedented corruption, and the casual cruelty and polarisation of rhetoric. While a weary and more conciliatory Trump could materialise – prospective Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer has mused about this possibility, and Trump himself initially suggested he was open to more bipartisan cooperation on certain issues – the president’s increasing heedlessness and clear signals that he takes the electoral catastrophe personally suggest that it is unlikely. 
It isn’t difficult to imagine ever-higher tariffs, escalation in Iran, even more intrusive and abusive immigration enforcement, and the further isolation and hobbling of Ukraine in favour of lucrative deals with Russia. A pressing question is whether Democrats will be able to build a coalition strong and integrated enough to constrain Trump through congressional action. Although there were instances of factionalisation and bitterness within the Democratic Party – especially in the Michigan Senate race, between the victorious Abdul El-Sayed and Haley Stevens, who lost the primary to him, over support for Israel – the party’s overall success in flipping traditionally Republican states was largely attributable to disciplined campaigns that stayed safely centrist and did not drift into shrill progressivism. Prominent progressives such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have become far more pragmatic. This suggests that despite recrimination and disarray within the party following Kamala Harris’s loss in the 2024 presidential election, Democrats could enjoy greater discipline and cohesion moving forward. How will this translate into action? Having tried and failed twice to convict Trump on impeachment charges during his first term, Democrats appear to have limited appetite for trying again and risking another failure. The more plausible course, which Democrats are keen to undertake, is intense congressional investigations into Trump’s enrichment in office and general breaking of norms, including ICE excesses. To sustain their present momentum into 2028 for another generationally crucial presidential election, however, they will have to prioritise addressing the grievances that powered their success in 2026: the high cost of living, damage to American democracy, and unnecessary and ineffective military intervention. Voluntary behavioural modification on Trump’s part is doubtful. But the midterm disaster for Republicans – notwithstanding protestations of defiance by current Senate Majority Leader John Thune, and Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio, who may become House Minority Leader – will have conclusively soured some of them on Trumpism. This factor may non-trivially increase bipartisan inclinations to constrain the president.
Trump may also find the judicial branch less helpful to him. His aggressive instrumentalisation of the Justice Department to target his personal and political enemies has met with broadly strong resistance from the lower federal courts, and the Supreme Court, though unprecedentedly permissive of executive action, will likely take note of the political tide in future decisions. Nevertheless, any notion that he will be a quiescent lame duck seems far-fetched.show more
